title: Peter Nagy, Gallerist Who Put Indian Contemporary Art on World Map, Dies at 67
excerpt: The American-born founder of Nature Morte, who moved to Delhi in 1992 and championed Bharti Kher, Jitish Kallat and a generation of Indian artists, has died after a long illness.
body:
• Peter Nagy, the American-born artist and founder of Nature Morte, has died at 67 after a long illness, the gallery confirmed on October 13.
  • Nagy co-founded Nature Morte in New York's East Village in 1982, moved to New Delhi in 1992, and relaunched the gallery there in 1997.
  • He is credited with launching or nurturing a generation of Indian contemporary stars, including Bharti Kher, Jitish Kallat, Subodh Gupta and L. N. Tallur.
  • Nature Morte's galleries in Delhi and Mumbai will remain open, in line with Nagy's stated wishes.

Peter Nagy, the American-born artist and gallerist whose Delhi gallery Nature Morte reshaped how Indian contemporary art was seen at home and abroad, has died at the age of 67. Nature Morte confirmed his death on October 13, saying, according to The Art Newspaper, that he passed away after a long illness.

From the East Village to New Delhi

Nagy was born in Bridgeport, Connecticut, in 1959 and studied communication design at the Parsons School of Design in New York, graduating in 1981. A year later he co-founded Gallery Nature Morte in Manhattan's East Village with fellow artist Alan Belcher. The small artist-run space became part of a wave of downtown galleries offering an alternative to SoHo and uptown, showing figures including Gretchen Bender, Vito Acconci, Cindy Sherman and Sherrie Levine before it closed in 1988.

As an artist, Nagy worked with photocopied logos, museum floor plans and images from art history, making handmade work that looked machine-made. His Xerox collages and later Cancer paintings examined consumerism and the flood of reproduced images, and his work entered the collections of the Whitney Museum of American Art, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Brooklyn Museum and the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles. A survey of that early work was shown at Jeffrey Deitch in New York in 2020.

Building Nature Morte in India

Nagy began travelling to India after the New York gallery closed, moved to New Delhi in 1992, and reopened Nature Morte there in 1997 as both a commercial gallery and a curatorial project for contemporary South Asian art. He remained one of the very few foreign-born dealers working in the field, and peers credit his outsider eye with spotting artists whose work would travel internationally.

"It doesn't matter whether people care now — they will in 15 years."

— Peter Nagy, recalled by Aparajita Jain, Nature Morte partner and executive director

Writing in Mint, curator and writer Meera Menezes described Nagy as a catalyst for Indian art, noting his role in nurturing Bharti Kher, Jitish Kallat, Manisha Parekh, Subodh Gupta and L. N. Tallur. Kher, his friend of 30 years, called him a visionary and said India was his spiritual home. Nature Morte's roster grew to 41 artists, including Raqs Media Collective, Reena Saini Kallat and Imran Qureshi.

The gallery also worked beyond Delhi. It ran a Kolkata space with New York's Bose Pacia gallery from 2006 to 2009 and a Berlin outpost from 2008 to 2013, opened a Mumbai space in Colaba in 2024, and moved into a new Delhi space in Gulmohar Park earlier this year. In recent years it gave artists including Alicja Kwade and Ai Weiwei their first exhibitions in the region, and it remains a regular exhibitor at Frieze London.

What happens next

Nature Morte said its galleries will stay open, as Nagy wished, rather than closing in mourning. A show marking 30 years of Nature Morte in India, The Evolution of the Soothsayer, which Nagy had been overseeing, was due to open at the Gulmohar Park space in the coming weeks. More background on his life and work is available on his Wikipedia page.

For Indian and diaspora collectors who came of age with the contemporary boom of the 2000s, Nagy's death closes a formative chapter: the dealer who imported a New York gallery model to Delhi, then used it to carry Indian artists to New York, Berlin and London in return.
